During mind-blanking, however, subjects may have gone beyond "autopilot" and stopped altogether moving their eyes across the screen and pressing keys to advance to the next paragraph, thus allowing them to recover when their thoughts returned to the self-paced text.

Are Mind Blanking Reports Valid?

The lack of correlation between mind-blanking and mind-wandering rates, and their divergent correlations with comprehension of self-paced reading, provide evidence for the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports, insofar as they reflect subjects distinguishing the experiences of content-absent from content-laden off-task thought. Below, we first consider other positive evidence for construct validity in the literature, which similarly indicates some distinctions between mind-blanking and mind-wandering (and on-task thought) reports. We then discuss other evidence that may be more problematic for claims of validity.

Positive Evidence for Construct Validity

Several lines of behavioral evidence provisionally suggest that probed mind-blanking reports may be valid. In multiple samples, mind-blanking propensity has been more strongly related to ADHD symptoms than is mind-wandering during laboratory attention tasks (such as the go/no-go "Sustained Attention to Response Task" [SART]; Robertson et al., 1997). In Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 7 undergraduates, rates of mind-blanking correlated significantly with self-reported ADHD symptoms whereas rates of mind-wandering did not (Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024). Further, in adults assessed for ADHD via diagnostic interview, those high in ADHD symptomology (n = 15) had higher mind-blanking rates, but not mind-wandering rates, than did those low in ADHD symptomology (n = 25; Van den Driessche et al., 2017, Study 2). In children aged 6-12, the findings are more complex (perhaps suggestive of self-report challenges with young children): Those with untreated ADHD showed higher mind-blanking rates than those with pharmacologically treated ADHD and healthy and clinical controls (ns = 19-20 in each group), but those with treated ADHD showed higher mind-wandering rates than did those with untreated ADHD and controls (Van den Driessche et al., 2017, Study 1). Only one study that we're aware of, in adults, found that a diagnosed ADHD group showed both more mind-blanking and more mind-wandering during the SART than did controls (Madiouni et al., 2020).

More limited evidence suggests that mind-blanking and mind-wandering may also be differentially associated with in-the-moment SART performance. Specifically, mind-blanking reports were immediately preceded by more "go" trial misses than were mind-wandering reports (with both preceded by more misses than were on-task thought reports; Andrillon et al., 2021; Munoz-Musat et al., 2025 2 ), and mind-blanking was preceded by go-trial sequences with longer RTs than was mind-wandering (Andrillon et al., 2021; Munoz-Musat et al., 2025). Such findings might indicate that mind-blanking is associated with a more complete withdrawal of external processing than is mind-wandering. Evidence also suggests, however, that mind-blanking and mind-wandering reports are preceded by similar false-alarm ("no go") error rates (Andrillon et al., 2021; Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024; Munoz-Musat et al., 2025), and by similar RT variability over the preceding four go-task trials (Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024).

We note that these positive findings were not, as far as we're aware, predicted by theory.

There doesn't seem to be a compelling or coherent explanation for why mind-blanking and mind-wandering propensities might be differentially related to medicated versus unmedicated ADHD in children, or why mind-blanking should be more strongly associated with ADHD symptoms in adults than is mind-wandering, or why mind-blanking might be more strongly associated with target misses and mean RTs than is mind-wandering, but not with other performance indicators like false alarms or RT variability. From the nomothetic span approach to construct validity, however, which relies on patterns of associations versus dissociations among measures of similar versus dissimilar constructs (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955; Embretson, 1983), finding any replicable differences between mind-blanking and mind-wandering suggests that people's self-reports are reflecting distinctions of some kind between these experiences.

The validity of mind-blanking reports is also partially supported by fMRI findings, but evidence is mixed. During attempts to "think of nothing" with occasional thought probes, periods preceding mind-blanking reports showed deactivation in Broca's area and left anterior insula relative to mind-wandering periods, but only with a liberal post-hoc significance threshold and not with planned conservative thresholds (Kawagoe et al., 2019). Moreover, during rest, regionof-interest analyses found deactivations preceding mind-blanking versus mind-wandering reports in ventromedial PFC/anterior cingulate cortex, but no differences in Broca's area (Boulakis et al., 2023). Rather than focusing on a priori regions of interest, connectivity analyses during rest indicated greater global signal amplitude preceding mind-blanking reports versus mind-wandering reports, and periods preceding mind-blanking reports consistently showed a connectivity pattern like that associated with slow-wave sleep (Mortaheb et al., 2022).

Finally, EEG findings from three thought-probe studies may also (provisionally) imply construct validity of mind-blanking reports. During the SART, mind-blanking periods produced slow wave signatures more similar to sleep than did mind-wandering (Andrillon et al., 2021; Munoz-Musat et al., 2025), and mind-blanking was characterized by an absence of late processing (i.e., virtually absent P3b component) in contrast to mind-wandering and on-task thought (Munoz-Musat et al., 2025). During rest, balanced random forest classifiers based on EEG, electrocardiogram, pupillometry, and electrodermal data taken before each thought probe achieved above-chance accuracy in classifying mind-blanking periods versus other off-task thought periods in known subjects, but no classifier successfully did so in out-of-sample subjects (Boulakis et al., 2025).

Many of the neuroscience results described above are suggestive, particularly those associating mind-blanking reports with sleep-like slow waves. Such findings are helpful to establishing construct validity, by linking mind-blanking self-reports with more "objective" indicators of experience. But given some inconsistencies in findings across and within studies (such as those for Broca's area), the small samples (Ns < 40), and the lack of independent replications so far, more consistent and robust evidence will be needed from future neuroscience studies to compellingly support the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports.

Problematic Evidence for Construct Validity

Some findings suggest skepticism is warranted about mind-blanking reports. Ward and Wegner (2013, Experiments 2a and 3a) used the self-catch method (Schooler et al., 2004) to capture off-task experiences during reading. Subjects pressed a button whenever they spontaneously realized they were off-task; they had to then indicate whether they had been mindwandering or mind-blanking, followed by a dichotomous question to confirm or disconfirm their reports ("Are you sure?"). Mind-wandering reports were more frequent than mind-blanking reports, but most relevant here is the percentage of corrections made for both mental states. Of the total mind-blanking reports in Experiments 2a and 3a, respectively, 81% and 86% were confirmed, compared to 97% and 96% confirmed mind-wandering reports. Initial mind-blanking reports were corrected considerably more often than mind-wandering reports, which were confirmed nearly every time. Mind-blanking reports, then, although frequently confirmed, were made with less certainty than mind-wandering reports.

We see further evidence for an apparent hesitation around mind-blanking reports in Kawagoe et al. (2019). Here, subjects tried to think of nothing during an fMRI scan and respond to occasional thought probes. When subjects made a mind-blanking report, they were asked whether they were truly mind-blanking or just trying to follow the instructions. Overall, subjects reported mind-blanking to 57% of the probes. The follow-up confirmation question reduced the rate dramatically, to 32%. The sharp decline in mind-blanking reports after double-checking once again indicates uncertainty around mind-blanking experiences.

One explanation for low confidence in mind-blanking reports is the difficulty that subjects might face in recalling their thoughts, especially considering that people often mindwander without awareness until they are interrupted by a probe (e.g., Schooler et al. 2004; Smallwood et al., 2008). In fact, Mathews et al. (2024) provided evidence that people can nearly immediately forget their off-task thought content. Subjects completed hard or easy versions of the SART, or another sustained attention task (Seli et al., 2013), while responding to thought probes that included the following response options: 1) on task, 2) off task and I do remember what I was thinking about, 3) off-task but I do not remember what I was thinking about. Subjects frequently reported being off task but unable to remember what they were thinking about (Ms ≈ 15-20% of all responses; see also Yeo et al., 2025).

An occasional lack of meta-awareness during mind-wandering episodes may disrupt the subsequent recall of off-task thought content. In such instances of not knowing what one was thinking, or "drawing a blank" in recollection, the uncertainty about experience might be perceived by subjects as mind-blanking (Mathews et al. 2024). This might be especially likely if thought probes provide an option to report mind-blanking but not to report uncertainty or a failure to recall. That is, the inability to produce or access information (as in the tip-of-thetongue phenomenon), or the unawareness of what one was just thinking about, may lead some subjects to mistakenly report their prior experience as mind-blanking. Reporting conscious experiences is constrained by the response options available, which may skew the findings and conclusions (see, e.g., Fell, 2022; Kane et al., 2021; Weinstein, 2018). If probed mind-blanking studies do not provide response options to decipher between I-don't-know responses and other mental content (or lack thereof), then we cannot be confident that subjects truly experienced mind-blanking.

It may be surprising that few published mind-blanking studies have offered a "don't remember" response option on thought probes, especially considering the ambiguity surrounding self-reports and the mind-blanking phenomenon. Andrillion et al. (2021) and Munoz-Masat et al., 2025 found that 1.1% and 2.6%, respectively, of all probes elicited responses of "don't remember," which were then combined with mind-blanking reports as "mind-blanking" rates by the investigators (Corcoran et al., 2025, and Palhares et al., 2026, also combined these response options in "mind blanking" rates without reporting them separately). We suggest that these two options should not be used interchangeably. Relatedly, some mind-wandering studies have combined mind-blanking with other mental states within the same response option in their thought probes ("I am not very alert/My mind is blank"; e.g., Robison et al., 2018 Robison et al., , 2022;; Robison & Unsworth, 2018; Unsworth & Robison, 2018). If the field is interested in better understanding the mind-blanking phenomenon, it must do a better job of conceptualizing and measuring it.

Goals and Hypotheses

Despite growing scientific interest in mind-blanking experiences (for reviews, see Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Kaufmann et al., 2024), researchers have yet to rigorously test the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports. This is concerning, considering the possibility that mind-blanking reports may reflect uncertainty or a lack of awareness of one's thoughts, rather than a true experience of nothingness, leading to possibly erroneous conclusions about mind-blanking phenomena (for related concerns, see Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Fell, 2022).

The present study, therefore, assessed the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports in four online asynchronous studies. Specifically, we tested whether mind-blanking experiences are reported consistently across different varieties of thought probes, some of which allowed subjects to indicate a lack of certainty about their preceding conscious state.

We conducted Study 1a using thought probes within the SART and replicated it in Study 1b using a longer SART to decrease on-task thought reports (and a larger participant sample to increase statistical power). We then conducted Study 2 using an easier "vigilance" version of the SART and increased the duration of the stimuli to reduce the task demands, reduce on-task thoughts, and increase reporting of off-task thoughts. Finally, Study 3 was conducted to investigate further what the "blank" in mind-blanking may have meant to subjects; that is, did subjects use mind-blanking to refer to a complete lack of experience, or rather a lack of clear and specific thoughts but with some subjective experience (Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Fell, 2022)?

Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 all tested whether probes that differed in response options would yield significantly different rates of mind-blanking and I-don't-know reports. Specifically, these between-subject studies presented subjects with one of three different thought probes during the SART. An "I-don't-know" option was provided to distinguish between I-don't-know and mind-

blanking experiences in the Mind-blanking & I-don't-know (MB & IDK) probe-type condition.

Rates of mind-blanking were compared between this MB & IDK condition and a condition including only a "mind-blanking" option (MB but no IDK condition). Additionally, rates of Idon't-know reports were compared between conditions that either included only the "I-don'tknow" response option (IDK but no MB condition) or both relevant options (MB & IDK condition).

Our reasoning was that, if subjects sometimes inaccurately report experiences of mindblanking because they forgot or were unsure of their previous thoughts (Mathews et al., 2024), then rates of mind-blanking and I-don't-know responses should differ systematically across conditions that vary in including "I-don't-know" and "mind-blanking" response options. If mindblanking experiences are often miscategorized given the probe options, then mind-blanking rates should selectively drop when subjects are also offered an "I-don't-know" response. Since there were response options to distinguish between I-don't-know and mind-blanking experiences in the MB & IDK condition, we expected rates of mind-blanking to be lower in this condition compared to the one that only provided the "mind-blanking" but no "I-don't-know" response option.

Moreover, if some mind-blanking reports arise from I-don't-know experiences, then this should also selectively increase I-don't-know report rates in the condition without the "mindblanking" option (IDK but no MB condition): Reports that would have been miscategorized as blanking should now be accurately reported, resulting in higher rates of I-don't-know reports. In comparison, subjects in the MB & IDK condition should produce lower rates of I-don't-know reports compared to subjects in the IDK but no MB condition due to the possibility of reporting Idon't-know experiences as blanking in the former.

In prior studies (Kawagoe et al. 2019; Ward & Wegner, 2013), mind-blanking reports have been corrected more often than mind-wandering reports, suggesting ambiguity associated with the experience of mind-blanking. Accordingly, we administered confidence ratings after each thought report in the MB but no IDK condition in Experiments 1a, 1b, and 2, and predicted that confidence in mind-blanking reports would be lower than for other off-task thought reports.

Finally, as argued above, a lack of clarity about an immediately preceding conscious experience (i.e., uncertain or inaccessible thoughts) might result in subjects defaulting to reporting mind-blanking, even if they had not actually been devoid of conscious experience (Mathews et al., 2024). If some mind-blanking reports derive from uncertainty rather than a true "blanking" of consciousness, then subjects might take more time to report mind-blanking than other off-task experiences because they are searching for content or waiting for necessary information to accumulate. The same should be true for "don't know" responses, as subjects must engage in a search process if the preceding thoughts or experience do not immediately come to mind. Thus, we hypothesized that mind-blanking RTs and I-don't-know RTs would be similar, with both significantly longer than those for other thought category reports.

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 15

To preview, the findings from Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 indicated that mind-blanking reports were not simply mislabeled reports of being unsure about one's prior experience. We therefore designed Study 3 to improve our understanding of what specific kinds of experiences people might have meant to convey when they reported a "blank mind." To do so, we separated the mind-blanking phenomenon into two separate and more specific thought report categories, within subjects, to assess their respective reporting rates.

Studies 1a and 1b

Studies 1a and 1b received ethics approval from the UNC Greensboro Institutional Review Board (IRB; protocol number 23-278).

Method

The methods for Studies 1a and 1b were identical except that Study 1b had a larger participant sample and a longer SART to reduce on-task report rates observed in Study 1a (Ms ≈ .75), and to potentially increase the low mind-blanking rates from Study 1a.

Sample Size Justification

As stated in our preregistrations (https://osf.io/kxgqy/), we conducted a sensitivity analysis using G*Power for Study 1a ("Mind Blanking Exploratory Online Study") based on our resources for paying subjects. A t-test comparing pairwise independent means with 150 subjects in each thought-probe-type condition (N = 450 across three conditions) yields 80% power (alpha = .05) for effect size d = 0.32, 90% power for d = 0.38, and 95% power for d = 0.42.

We preregistered a larger sample for Study 1b ("Mind Blanking Exploratory Online Study, Follow-Up Study 2"). A sensitivity analysis for a t-test comparing pairwise independent means indicated that 250 subjects in each of the 3 conditions (N = 750 total) yields 80% power for d = .25, 90% power for d = .29, and 95% power for d = .32.

Subjects

Four hundred seventy-one subjects completed Study 1a and 786 completed Study 1b via the online recruitment site, Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/). Via Prolific prescreening, we limited the participating age range to 18-40 years, due to the decline in mind-wandering rates for older adults (e.g., Jackson & Balota, 2012; McVay et al., 2013); participant ages (after exclusions) for Studies 1a and 1b were M = 31.40, SD = 5.71, and M = 31.39, SD = 5.72, respectively. We also prescreened for U.S. residency, English as a first language, obtaining at least a high school diploma (or equivalent), and having a ≥ 95% study approval rate.

The sample for Study 1a was 35% female, 62% male, and 3% gender nonconforming.

Regarding race/ethnicity, the sample was 65% White, 10% South Asian, 8% multiracial, 8% Hispanic or Latino, 5% African American, 2% East Asian, 1% Native or Alaskan American, and less than 1% Middle Eastern or Native Hawaiian. Eligible subjects were compensated $4 (rate of $12/hr) for the 20-min study. For Study 1b, the sample was 50% female, 48% male, and 2% gender nonconforming. Regarding race/ethnicity, the sample was 57% White, 20% African American, 8% multiracial, 5% East Asian, 5% Hispanic or Latino, 3% South Asian, 1% Native or Alaskan American, and less than 1% Middle Eastern or Native Hawaiian. Eligible subjects for Study 1b were compensated $6.50 ($13/hr) for the 30-min study.

We dropped data from seven subjects in Study 1a and 16 subjects in Study 1b after exclusions (described below).

Sustained Attention To Response Task (SART)

The SART go/no-go task was programmed in Gorilla (https://gorilla.sc/); the programs for Studies 1a and 1b are openly available at: https://app.gorilla.sc/openmaterials/859045. The study could only be completed on a desktop or laptop computer.

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 17

Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for any animal name and to withhold responses ("no-go") for any crop (fruit or vegetable) name; animal names occurred on 90% of the task trials. All words were centrally presented onscreen for 272 ms followed by a pattern mask (XXXXXXXXXXXX) for 1224 ms. Subjects could press the spacebar during the presentation of either the word or the mask to record their responses. Before the start of the task, subjects completed ten practice trials with boy names ("go") and girl names ("no-go").

For Study 1a, subjects completed 480 critical trials divided into four seamless blocks of 120 (16 unanalyzed buffer trials preceded the critical trials). The full stimulus list included 144 unique animal names and 16 crop names. For Study 1b, two additional trial blocks were added to the SART, for a total of 720 critical trials. The stimulus list for Study 1b included 214 unique animal names and 24 crop names. In both experiments, each stimulus was pseudo-randomly presented three times per block; all stimuli were presented in the same order to all subjects.

Each block also presented six thought probes to capture subjects' immediately preceding thoughts; these were randomized and then presented in the same order to everyone. Each thought-probe screen presented the following: "What were you just thinking about? Please press a number on the keyboard," with the probe response options appearing below. Six probe options were consistent across all experimental conditions; italicized text below represents the verbatim descriptions from the on-screen instructions (response options that differed across conditions will be discussed subsequently): 1. The task/task performance ("If you were thinking about the computer task, or about how you are doing on it.") ; 2. Everyday things/personal worries ("Select this if your thoughts were about normal, routine things you did recently or that you'll be doing later, or about big or small life concerns or worries.") ; 3. Current state of being ("Select this if you were thinking about your state of mind or feelings, such as thinking about being sleepy, Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 18 cheerful, hungry, curious, or bored.") ; 4. Daydreams/fantasies ("Select this for fantasies or thoughts disconnected from reality, like thoughts about flying, or being at the beach.") ; 5.

External environment ("Select this if you were thinking about something in your environment, other than the task, like sights or sounds in the room."). "Other" was also an option for all conditions, for thoughts that did not fall into any other provided categories ("Select 'other'' ONLY if your thoughts don't fit the other options."). Additional thought responses were dependent on experimental conditions, described below.

The task instructions presented a description of each thought-probe option before the start of SART. Each probe remained onscreen for 10 s, regardless of when or whether the participant answered. Study 1a presented 24 probes and Study 1b presented 36.

Thought Probe Conditions

The Gorilla program randomly assigned subjects to one of three conditions that differed in thought probe response-menu options (see Figure 1); italicized text again represents the verbatim descriptions from the on-screen instructions. The MB but no IDK condition included a mind-blanking ("blank mind") response option (#6; "You were not thinking about the task or anything else at all-Your mind was a complete blank."), and each probe response was followed by a confidence rating screen. The confidence screen asked subjects to rate their confidence in their thought-report choice on a 1-5 scale, with the following labels, 1 ("not at all confident"), 2 ("somewhat confident"), 3 ("confident"), 4 ("very confident"), 5 ("extremely confident"). We included confidence ratings for only this condition because the "I-don't-know" response option in other conditions (see below) served the role of capturing low-confidence responses. The MB & IDK condition included both a "blank mind" option (#6) and a "don't know/can't report" option (#8; "If you don't know or can't recollect what your immediately preceding thoughts were Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 19 about"). Finally, the IDK but no MB condition had a "don't know/can't report" (#7) option but no "blank mind" option. Thought Probes by Condition MB but no IDK MB & IDK IDK but no MB

Procedures

After consenting to participate, subjects answered two simple free-response questions to filter out bots and extremely inattentive subjects. If subjects answered at least one question correctly, they proceeded to a demographics survey that inquired about their gender, age, birth year, race/ethnicity, and highest level of education. Then, they were informed about the purpose of our study and instructed to switch off their phones:

This study is about attention. The tasks involved will challenge your ability to stay focused. We hope the study will advance understanding of how attention works .

Before you start, please switch off and silence your phone/e-mail/music so you can focus. Thank you! During this study's tasks, we will occasionally ask what you were just thinking about. It's normal to sometimes lose focus during computer tasks. We want to know what you think about. The task will sometimes stop to ask what you were just thinking about, Note. MB = "mind-blanking" response option; IDK = "don't know/can't report" response option. in the instant before we asked. You will see a thought-choice menu. Please take stock of what your thoughts just were and choose the closest description.

An illustration of thought probe screen was then displayed. Each menu option and its description were then presented individually (with a minimum duration of 1500 ms before subjects could advance the screen). For the probe conditions that included a mind-blanking option, the instructions told subjects to select the "blank mind" option if, "…you were not thinking about the task or anything else at all-Your mind was a complete blank" (after Ward & Wegner, 2013). For conditions that included an I-don't-know option, the instructions told subjects to select the "don't know/can't report" response option if, "you don't know or can't recollect what your immediately preceding thoughts were about."

After the presentation of all probe options, subjects were reminded to choose the option that matched the content of their thoughts in the instant before the menu appeared and to use the numbers located at the top of the keyboard to respond to the probe. They were then quizzed on these instructions: "When responding about your thoughts, what time frame should you report your thoughts from? 1) Since the very beginning of the task, 2) The moment right before the thought menu appeared, 3) Over the last 30-60 seconds, and 4) Since the last time a thought menu screen appeared." They were reminded of the instructions if they failed to answer correctly (with response option 2).

Study 1b also included instructions to inform subjects that reporting off-task thoughts would not result in their submission being rejected. These instructions indicated that thought probes are not attention checks that determine payment, but that subjects must complete enough of them to not have their study submission rejected for missing crucial questions.

Subjects in the MB but no IDK condition received additional instructions on the confidence rating. After each thought report, subjects were asked to rate how confident they were Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 21 in their report by choosing a number on the keyboard on a number scale from 1 (not at all confident) to 5 (extremely confident).

Next, subjects received SART instructions and completed 10 practice trials with a thought probe at the end. To ensure subjects read and understood the instructions of the SART with animal (go) and crop (no-go) stimuli, they had to first answer the following comprehension question: "When performing this task, which words should you NOT press any key for?"

Response options were: 1) animal names, 2) girl names, 3) crop names, 4) boy names. If subjects did not select the correct answer (3), they were reminded of the instructions and quizzed again.

Then, they moved forward to the real trials, which lasted approximately 15 min in Study 1a and 20 min in Study 1b.

After completing the SART, Study 1a subjects in the two probe conditions with mindblanking response options answered the following exploratory question by pressing the corresponding number on the keyboard (a programming error in Study 1b eliminated this question from the procedure):

One of the thought report options during the task was a blank mind to indicate that you were not thinking about anything at all -your mind was a complete blank. What do you believe about this experience? Please select the appropriate letter on the keyboard that corresponds to your choice.

1) It makes sense to me, I can believe that people experience this, and I've experienced this in everyday life.

2) It makes sense to me, I can believe that people experience this, but I am unsure about whether I've experienced this in everyday life.

3) It makes sense to me, I can believe that people experience this, but I believe that I have not experienced this in everyday life.

4) It does not make sense to me, I'm skeptical that people experience this, and I believe that I have not experienced this in everyday life.

All subjects in both studies then answered several data exclusion questions. The first was, "How noisy (people, music, TV) were your immediate surroundings while completing this study?" They responded on a scale with these labels: not at all noisy, slightly noisy, moderately noisy, or extremely noisy. The next question asked, "How distracted were you by things in your Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 22 immediate environment while completing this study?" The same scale range was displayed as the previous question, but with "distracted" substituted for "noisy." Next, they answered, "During the study, how often did you interact with 1) phone calls (calls or texts), 2) email or social media, 3) video games. Each of these three questions presented a 4-point response scale ranging from Never to All the time. Lastly, they were asked: "How sleepy were you at the beginning of this study?" Subjects responded using a scale ranging from 1 (not at all sleepy) to 4 (extremely sleepy).

Data Exclusions

As preregistered (https://osf.io/kxgqy/), to ensure that retained subjects were focused on the task, all data were dropped from subjects, case-wise, if: (a) they responded to fewer than 20 of the 24 probes in Study 1a, or to fewer than 30 of the 36 probes for Study 1b, before the 10 s probe-response deadline, or; (b) they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or; (c) they responded to any of the three media-multitasking questions with "Most of the time" or "All of the time." In Study 1b, we also prescreened anyone who had completed Study 1a.

Results

All analyses for Study 1a and 1b were conducted in R (version 4.3,1, R Foundation for

Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) and thus we deviated from our preregistration to use JASP. All reported inferential tests reported below were 2-sided, with an alpha level of .05.

We collected data from 471 subjects in Study 1a. As preregistered, data from three subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three media-multitasking questions, or both. Also as preregistered, data from four other subjects in Study 1a were dropped because they responded to fewer than 20 thought probes. We also excluded one subject's data who somehow received an extra thought probe (we did not anticipate this possibility in our preregistration), resulting in a final sample size of N = 463. The MB but no IDK condition included n = 150 subjects, the MB & IDK condition had n = 158 subjects, and the

Study 1b tested N = 786 before exclusions. As preregistered, we dropped data from eight subjects because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three media-multitasking questions, or both.

Also as preregistered, we excluded data from eight additional subjects who responded to fewer than 30 thought probes (out of 36), resulting in a final sample size of N = 770 for Study 1b. The MB but no IDK condition included n = 253 subjects, the MB & IDK condition had n = 262 subjects, and the IDK but no MB condition included n = 255 subjects.

Completed Thought Probes

Study 1a presented subjects with 24 thought probes; after subject exclusions described above, the M number of probes that subjects responded to within the 10 s deadline ranged across conditions from 23.72 (SD = 0.63) to 23.78 (SD = 0.54). Study 1b presented 36 thought probes; across the three conditions, the M number of probes that retained subjects responded varied between M = 35.63 (SD = 0.93) to 35.67 (SD = 0.95).

Comparisons of Thought-Report Rates

The report rate of each thought category was calculated as the number of probes that a subject endorsed from a thought category divided by the total number of probes the subject Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 24 responded to before the response deadline. Table 1 presents the mean rates of all endorsed mental states in all probe-type conditions for Study 1a and Study 1b. Contrary to our predictions, mind-blanking rates in both studies appeared very similar for the MB but no IDK condition and the MB & IDK condition (Study 1a, Ms = .043 and .036, respectively; Study 1b, Ms = .053 and .045, respectively); as well, rates of I-don't-know responses were similarly-and extremelylow in both relevant probe conditions in both studies (Ms < .01).

We preregistered that we would analyze probe-condition differences in mind-blanking report rates via t-tests. However, the low mind-blanking rates we observed were indicative of over-dispersion; as shown in Figure 2, most subjects reported no instances of mind-blanking and so the distributions were extremely skewed. T-tests are inappropriate for such severely skewed and zero-inflated data, so we deviated from our preregistration and instead analyzed mindblanking reports as a count variable, as appropriate for an alternative analytic approach. For Study 1a, M count = 0.93, SD = 2.28 (M = 0.84, SD = 2.47 for the MB but no IDK condition, and and I-don't-know (IDK) report rates by probe-type condition and study (Panel A = Study 1a; Panel B = Study 1b). Panel A Panel B Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 27

Thus, we conducted a generalized linear negative binomial analysis to account for the overdispersion of counts using the MASS package in R (glm.nb function; Venables & Ripley, 2002). For these models, we converted probe-type condition to a factor and treated mindblanking as a count variable. Recall that we expected rates of mind-blanking to be higher in the in Study 1a, b = 0.14 [-1.27, 1.56], SE = .72, p = .848, or in Study 1b, b = .17 [-.53, .88], SE = .36, p = .634. The dispersion was fixed in the negative binomial model, with a dispersion ratio = 0.97 for Study 1a and 1.19 for Study 1b.

Contrary to our hypotheses, then, neither mind-blanking report counts, nor I-don't-know report counts, varied significantly with different probe options. Allowing subjects to make Idon't-know reports did not selectively reduce mind-blanking reports, and allowing subjects to make mind-blanking reports did not selectively reduce I-don't-know reports. Any actual effect of probe type is likely weak and thus meta-awareness failures are unlikely to drive blanking reports.

Confidence Ratings

We predicted subjects would rate their mind-blanking reports with low confidence, and with lower confidence than other thought-content reports. On the contrary, subjects who endorsed at least one mind-blanking experience were generally confident in their reports, M = 3.52 (SD = 1.28; n = 58) in Study 1a, and M = 3.69 (SD = 1.20; n = 107) in Study 1b; these mean values fall between the scale's verbal labels of "confident" (3) and "very confident" (4). Table 2 presents the M confidence ratings for every thought-report category for each experiment; Figure 3 displays raincloud plots for mind-blanking confidence ratings for both studies and shows that each study's modal rating average was 5 (out of 5; labeled "extremely confident").

As preregistered, we conducted pairwise comparisons using t-tests for within-person comparisons (with Holm corrections) to test for differences in confidence ratings across thoughtreport types. We also report Bayes Factors (BFs), using the BayesFactor package (Morey & Rouder, 2018), to compare performance of competing models; null models reflected a Cauchy distribution centered around 0 with a scaling parameter of 0.707. We interpreted BF10 < 0.33 (1/3) as providing modest evidence for the null relative to the alternative hypothesis, BF10 > 3.0 as providing modest evidence for the alternative hypothesis relative to the null, BF10 < 0.10

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 29 (1/10) as providing strong evidence for the null relative to the alternative hypothesis, and BF10 > 10 providing strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis relative to the null. two comparisons, BFs suggested modest to strong evidence that the data were more likely under than null than the alternative hypothesis).

On-task confidence was also significantly higher than daydream confidence, t(37) = 3.97, p < .001, d = 0.64, BF10 = 86.472, and current state confidence, t(68) = 3.76, p < .001, d = 0.45, BF10 = 65.426.

Study 1b showed a similar pattern: Mind-blanking confidence was significantly lower than on-task confidence, t(101) = -5.74, p < .001, d = 0.57, BF10 > 1000, but not significantly different from daydream confidence, t(54) = 0.30, p = .765, d = 0.04, BF10 = 0.076, or current state confidence, t(75) = -2.14, p = .360, d = 0.25, BF10 = 1.076 (BFs suggested modest evidence that the data were more likely under the null than the alternative hypothesis for only daydreams).

On-task confidence was also significantly higher than current state confidence, t(138) = 7.06, p < .001, d = 0.60, BF10 > 1000, and daydream confidence, t(95) = 5.99, p < .001, d = 0.60, BF10 > 1000.

As a non-preregistered exploratory analysis, we examined the correlation between confidence ratings and mind-blanking rates to investigate whether subjects with fewer mindblanking experiences were less confident in their blanking reports and vice versa. We preregistered for a different correlational analysis that we would report both Kendall's tau and Pearson's product-moment correlations because the skewness for the mind-blanking rates for Study 1a and Study 1b were 5.346 (SE = 0.139) and 4.380 (SE = 0.108), respectively, making tau more appropriate. In the interest of space, however, we will only report Pearson's correlations when their statistical significance differs from tau's. In Study 1a, tau was not significant, τ(56) = .17, p = 0.101, but the Pearson's correlation was, r(56) = .30, [.05, .52], p = 0.021. The correlation was not significant in Study 1b, with a larger sample, τ(105) = .06, p = 0.423.

Probe Report RT

We hypothesized that mind-blanking reports reflect, at least sometimes or in part, instances where people have difficulty remembering or accessing their immediately preceding thought content or experiences. If true, then mind-blanking reports should be made with longer RTs than other varieties of off-task reports, perhaps with similar latencies as I-don't-know reports that also reflect uncertainty (note that we only preregistered this analysis for Study 2, after completing Studies 1a and 1b).

Table 3 presents the mean probe response latencies for each thought probe response category for subjects in the MB & IDK condition, where probes included all the thought probe categories of interest. We conducted pairwise comparisons via withinperson paired t-tests (with Holm corrections for multiple comparisons) to compare probe RTs between mind-blanking reports and those for other thought categories to examine whether subjects were especially slow to report mind-blanking. Note that these RT analyses, here and across all our subsequent experiments, should be interpreted cautiously because many subjects had very few observations for each thought type. Table 4 presents the statistical details for the comparison of interest. In Study 1a, mind-blanking RTs were significantly longer than those from only on-task reports (see Table 4). On-task RTs were significantly shorter than every other thought category, except for I-don't-know reports (in Study 1a), likely due to few observations for the latter. Mindblanking report RTs and I-don't-know report RTs were not statistically different from one another in Study 1a or Study 1b, although mean RTs were 440 and 640 ms shorter, respectively, for mind-blanking than I-don't-know reports. Contrary to our hypothesis, however, mindblanking reports were not significantly slower than other task-unrelated thought reports, and BFs did not indicate modest evidence for either the null or alternative hypotheses. The lack of Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 33 significant RT differences here challenges our hypothesis that subjects reporting mind-blanking would initially attempt to retrieve an experience but, failing that, would make a delayed "blanking" report that reflected failed meta-consciousness or uncertainty.

Instead, it appears that subjects readily apprehended and reported a state of having no thoughts or experience.

SART Performance

To examine the association between mind-blanking propensity and SART performance (indicated by dʹ and within-person response time variability on go-trials [RTsd]; see Kane, Smeekens et al., 2021; Welhaf & Kane, 2024b; Welhaf et al., 2025), we assessed their correlation, collapsed over all probe-type conditions. As preregistered for our performance-based analyses, data were dropped from all subjects with < 70% accuracy on go trials, indicative that they did not understand the task, and data for any subjects whose value was outside the Median +/-3*IQR were censored to the Median +/-3*IQR for both studies. (Although we also preregistered in-the-moment performance analyses, comparing intrasubject RT variability and accuracy on trials preceding mind-blanking versus on-task thought reports, we did not conduct these analyses because not enough subjects reported sufficient instances of mind-blanking to provide robust results across our experiments; most subjects reported no mind-blanking at all, and most of those who did only reported one or two instances.)

In Study 1a, M RTsd = 124.27 (SD = 41.37) and M dʹ = 2.56 (SD = 0.98); mind-blanking rates were not significantly correlated with RTsd, τ(295) = .03, p = 0.501, but were (weakly) significantly correlated with dʹ, τ(295) = -.13, p = 0.004. Subjects with higher mind-blanking rates performed the SART less accurately. TUT rates (M = .24, SD = .24), reflecting off-task content, were significantly (but also weakly) correlated with both RTsd, r(449) = .13, p = .005 and with dʹ, r(449) = -.12 p = .009.

In Study 1b, M RTsd = 130.66 (SD = 43.60) and M dʹ = 2.50 (SD = 1.07). Here, with a larger sample, mind-blanking rates were not significantly correlated with either RTsd, τ(491) = .04, p = 0.196, or dʹ, τ(491) = -.03, p = .360. Although TUT rates (M = .26, SD = .23) were similarly not significantly correlated with RTsd, r(738) = .06, p = .094, they were again significantly (weakly) correlated with dʹ, r(738) = -.11, p = .002.

Post-SART Mind-Blanking Questionnaire

We evaluated whether subjects were accepting or skeptical of mind-blanking experiences. In Study 1a, the post-SART exploratory question indicated that 68.5% of subjects (n = 308 in the two probe conditions with a mind-blanking response option) reported that the mindblanking phenomenon "makes sense" to them and they believe they have experienced it in everyday life; an additional 24.3% indicated that the phenomenon "makes sense" to them, whether or not they had experienced it. Only 7.1% of subjects indicated that mind-blanking doesn't make sense to them and that they're skeptical that others experience it. (As noted earlier, we were unable to collect data for this question in Study 1b due to a programming error.) Most subjects were reportedly accepting of the mind-blanking phenomenon.

Post-SART Sleepiness Ratings

Lastly, as a preregistered secondary analysis to follow up on the apparent link between mind-blanking and signatures of sleep (e.g., Andrillon et al., 2021; Mortaheb et al., 2022; see also Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025), as well as self-reported sleepiness (Madiouni et al., 2020), we found a (weak) positive correlation between sleepiness ratings and mind-blanking rates overall in Study 1a, τ(306) = .14, p = .006. The weak significant correlation replicated in Study 1b, with a larger sample, τ(513) = .12, p = .003.

Discussion

Studies 1a and 1b examined the construct validity of mind-blanking reports using different probe response options across three conditions. Both studies indicated that, on average, adults experience mind-blanking infrequently in an online-experiment context. The mind-blanking rates here (M rates ≈ .05) were generally a bit lower than those from prior laboratory studies (typical Ms = .10-.15; e.g., Andrillon et al., 2021; Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024; Ward & Wegner, 2013), perhaps due to the online setting or participant sample (or both).

We expected to observe the condition without the "I-don't-know" response option to be associated with a significantly higher rate (or predicted log count) of mind-blanking reports, as evidence that subjects frequently mis-categorize I-don't-know experiences as mind-blanking.

The results indicated, however, that the two experimental conditions , MB & IDK and MB but no IDK, did not differ significantly in predicting the log counts of mind-blanking in either Study 1a or Study 1b (nor did the MB & IDK and IDK but not MB conditions differ in counts of I-don'tknow reports in either study).

It seems that if there were an actual effect of probe type in the population, it was not large or robust enough for us detect in either experiment. Our findings therefore provide preliminary evidence that most mind-blanking reports do not represent covert I-don't-know experiences.

Similarly, in the probe-type condition that included confidence ratings, we expected that subjects would report mind-blanking episodes with significantly lower confidence than for other thought types, reflecting uncertainty about these reports. Subjects, instead, were generally confident in their mind-blanking reports, which were made with similar confidence to other offtask thought categories (i.e., current state of being and daydreams), but not to on-task reports, where confidence ratings were higher than all other thought report categories. Whatever participants meant by their "blank mind" reports, then, they were reasonably certain about them.

Finally, we did not find a significant correlation between mind-blanking rates and mind-blanking confidence ratings in Study 1a or Study 1b, so it's unlikely that high confidence only comes with reporting many mind-blanking experiences.

Although mind-blanking reports were made with similar latencies as I-don't-know reports, as hypothesized, mind-blanking-report RTs were not significantly longer than those for any content-laden TUT categories. Timely mind-blanking reports are inconsistent with our hypothesis that they may reflect subjects being unsure of their experiences and waiting for evidence to accumulate (or not) about their experience or thoughts before overtly expressing their uncertainty. Instead, mind-blanking experiences seemed to be apprehended and reportable no more slowly than content-laden TUTs. These RT analyses, although based on few observations for most subjects, provided some further support for the construct validity of mindblanking reports.

Finally, and also consistent with the possibility that momentary mind-blanking reports are valid, the vast majority subjects in Study 1a responded to a multiple-choice question that the mind-blanking phenomenon "makes sense" to them, whether or not they had experienced it in everyday life (although most did report having experienced it). Only a small minority indicated that they were generally skeptical about the mind-blanking phenomenon.

Regarding performance analyses, however, mind-blanking rates were not correlated with RTsd and were correlated with dʹ in only Study 1a and not the larger Study 1b. On one hand, these null results are surprising from the perspective that mind-blanking reports faithfully capture instances in which subjects were not experiencing the events around them (Ward & Wegner, 2013). On the other hand, the lack of correlation may have been driven from mind-blanking rates being so low. If fewer than half the participants ever experience mind-blanking, and most of those who do only experience it once or twice, then this should limit its measurable negative impact. We note that, replicating prior studies, TUT rate correlated negatively with dʹ in both studies (and with RTsd in Study 1a), suggesting the null mind-blanking effect on performance wasn't the result of an unusual participant sample.

Overall, then, the findings from Studies 1a and 1b mostly suggest that subjects don't generally mis-categorize a lack of meta-awareness of conscious states as mind-blanking experiences. Mind-blanking reports were made confidently (according to confidence ratings), and quickly (according to thought probe RTs), and their frequency did not drop in the condition that offered a probe-response option to indicate uncertainty. All these results provisionally support the validity of probed mind-blanking reports. As noted above, however, the lack of correlation between mind-blanking rates and SART performance might be problematic if we take mind-blanking reports at face value.

Although our results are, so far, suggestive of mind-blanking's construct validity, it is possible that we were unable to detect any significant probe-condition differences (if any did exist) in mind-blanking rates due to their low frequency in both studies, despite our efforts to increase off-task thinking in Study 1b versus Study 1a by lengthening the SART. Online Prolific subjects may be highly motivated due to monetary rewards (and fearful of losing those rewards via inattentiveness), which may influence them to stay mentally on task at higher rates compared to typical laboratory subjects, and so additional efforts to decrease on-task thinking and boost overall mind-blanking rates seem warranted.

Study 2

Low rates of mind-blanking and I-don't-know reports might have hurt our ability to detect any probe-condition differences, and our attempt to reduce on-task report rates had no measurable effect in Study 1b. We can't yet be certain, then, that mind-blanking reports are not truly I-don't-know responses in disguise (although high confidence ratings and timely probe responses support their construct validity). As a further attempt to decrease on-task experiences, we conducted Study 2 with a less demanding task because off-task thinking tends to increase with less demanding laboratory tasks (e.g., Matthews et al., 2024; Rummel & Boywitt, 2014; Seli et al., 2016). Study 2 administered a less demanding variation of the SART, which asked subjects to passively observe the word stimuli 90% of the time and respond only to the target category occurring 10% of the time, compared to the standard SART where subjects had to respond 90% of the time and inhibit responding 10% of the time. Further, we modestly increased the presentation duration of each word and pattern mask to slow the trial pacing, which also tends to increase off-task reports (e.g., Antrobus, 1968 , Giambra, 1995; Welhaf & Kane, 2024a).

Method

Study 2 received ethics approval from the UNC Greensboro IRB (via modification of protocol number 23-278).

Sample Size Justification

As preregistered ("Mind Blanking Exploratory Online Study, Follow-Up Study 3"), we aimed to collect data from the same number of subjects (N = 750) in each condition (n = 250) as in Study 1b, with the same justification: For a t-test comparing pairwise independent means (alpha = .05, two-tailed), 250 subjects in each of the three conditions yields 80% power for d = .25, 90% power for d = .29, and 95% power for d = .32.

Subjects

Eight hundred and twenty U.S. Prolific subjects completed Study 2. Prescreening criteria did not change between studies, other than subjects who took part in Study 1a or Study 1b were not eligible to participate. Participant ages were (after exclusions) M = 30.03 years, SD = 5.73.

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 41

The sample for Study 2 was 46% female, 53% male, and 1% gender nonconforming.

Regarding race/ethnicity, the sample was 56% White, 25% African American, 7% multiracial, 6% Hispanic or Latino, 3% East Asian, 2% South Asian, and less than 1% Middle Eastern, or Native or Alaskan American. Two subjects identified (via free response) as "Asian" rather than using the provided response options to specify East or South Asian. Subjects were paid $7.75 upon completion; by design, the full-study median completion time was about 35 min, which was 5 min longer than Study 1b, resulting in a pay rate of about $13/hr.

Vigilance SART

The "vigilance" SART was programmed in Gorilla (https://gorilla.sc). The program for Study 2 is openly available at: https://app.gorilla.sc/openmaterials/859045.

As in McVay & Kane (2012a), the vigilance SART turned the go/no-go task into a "nogo/go" task, more typical of vigilance tasks of sustained attention. Rather than pressing the spacebar for most trials and withholding responses for the rare target category (as in the standard SART), subjects mostly withheld responses (90% of the time) and waited for rare targets to respond. Subjects were instructed to press the spacebar ("go") for the target category only, crops (fruits or vegetables), and to not press the spacebar ("don't-go") for animal names. All words were centrally presented onscreen for 352 ms (instead of 272 ms in Studies 1a and 1b) followed by a pattern mask (XXXXXXXXXXXX) for 1584 ms (instead of 1224 ms in Studies 1a and 1b).

These new, longer presentation durations preserved the ratio of word-to-mask durations from Studies 1a and 1b (and from prior laboratory studies; e.g., Kane et al., 2016). The number of stimuli, blocks, and trials was identical to Study 1b.

Procedures

The procedures for Study 2 were almost identical to Study 1b except for the go/no-go task instructions. Subjects completed 10 practice trials with boy (no-go) and girl (go) names, ending with a thought probe according to the condition assignment. The comprehension question after the main-task instructions was edited to: "When performing this task, which words should you respond to?" Response options were: 1) animal names, 2) girl names, 3) crop names, 4) boy names. If subjects failed to select "crop names," they were reminded of the instructions ("remember press key ONLY when you see a Crop name") and quizzed again. Then, subjects began the real trials, which lasted approximately 25 min, a 5-min increase from Study 1b due to the extended trial duration.

For Study 2, the programming error from Study 1b was fixed so that subjects in the two probe conditions with mind-blanking response options received the multiple-choice question about their beliefs about mind-blanking after completing the task. Subjects also responded to the same exclusion questions as in Studies 1a and 1b.

Results

We collected data from 820 subjects in Study 2 before exclusions (all preregistered, as in Studies 1a or 1b, unless otherwise noted). Data from six subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three media-multitasking questions, or both. We dropped data from 22 other subjects because they responded to fewer than 30 thought probes. Finally, although not preregistered (but consistent with Study 1a), data from two subjects were dropped because they somehow received more than 36 thought probes. After exclusions, the total sample size was N = 790. The MB but no IDK condition included n = 268 subjects, the MB & IDK condition had n = 262 subjects, and the IDK but no MB condition included n = 260 subjects.

Completed Thought Probes

Study 2 presented 36 thought probes in the SART. Across probe-type conditions, retained subjects responded to between M = 35.43 (SD = 1.06) and 35.63 (SD = 0.83) probes.

Comparisons of Thought-Report Rates

Table 5 presents the mean rates of all endorsed thought categories in all probe-type conditions for Study 2. On-task report rates were slightly lower than before, suggesting that our changes to the SART were marginally effective. The mind-blanking rate in the MB but no IDK condition was M = .064 (SD = .144), and in the MB & IDK condition was M = .053 (SD = .120).

As in Studies 1a and 1b, then, probe-type condition-and the inclusion versus exclusion of the "I-don't-know" reporting option-did not appear to substantially affect mind-blanking rates.

Because most subjects again reported no instances of mind-blanking, and mind-blanking rates were highly skewed, we conducted a generalized linear negative binomial analysis, with probe-type condition as the predictor, to account for overdispersion and to test whether the conditions differed in predicting mind-blanking report counts (this analysis was preregistered for Study 2); the overdispersion ratio was 10.389 for the standard Poisson model. The overall mindblanking count was, M = 2.07 (SD = 4.65); for the MB but no IDK condition, M = 2.24 (SD = 5.02), and for the MB & IDK condition, M = 1.89 (SD = 4.24). The two probe-type conditions were not significantly different in predicting the log counts of mind-blanking, b = -0.17 [-0.55, 0.21], SE = .20, p = .386. The dispersion was fixed after fitting the negative binomial model, with a dispersion ratio of 0.991.

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 44

Since I-don't-know report rates had similar distribution issues as mind-blanking rates, we also used a negative binomial model to test whether the probe-type conditions differed in predicting I-don't-know response counts, which had an overall M = 0.28 (SD = 1.30); for the IDK but no MB condition, M = 0.39 (SD = 1.70), and for the MB & IDK condition, M = 0.18 (SD = 0.67). The dispersion ratio was 5.06 for the standard Poisson model. Contrary to Study 1a and 1b, I-don't-know response counts were significantly higher in the IDK but no MB condition compared to the MB & IDK condition, b = 0.84 [0.15, 1.53], SE = 0.35, p = .017. (The dispersion was fixed when using the negative binomial model, with the ratio of 1.29.)

Specifically, the count of I-don't-know responses was expected to be 0.84 log units higher for IDK but no MB condition than for the MB & IDK condition. This is the only comparison across our studies, then, that has supported our prediction that when the mind-blanking response option is removed, subjects should report more I-don't-know experiences, indicative of subjects sometimes confusing mind-blanking with uncertainty about their experience (note again, however, that mind-blanking counts did not show a significant effect of probe type here). and I-don't-know (IDK) report rates by probe-type condition in Study 2.

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 47

Confidence Ratings

Raincloud plots for mind-blanking confidence ratings are shown in Figure 5; see Table 6 for M confidence ratings for every thought-report category. Recall that subjects in Study 1a and 1b who endorsed at least one mind-blanking experience were generally confident in their reports (confidence rating Ms = 3.52 and 3.69, respectively), and Study 2 yielded a similar but slightly higher rating, M = 3.91 (SD = 0.96; n = 111). Also as in Study 1a and 1b, the modal M confidence rating for mind-blanking reports was a 5 out of 5.

As preregistered, we again conducted pairwise comparisons via t-tests for within-person comparisons (with Holm corrections) to evaluate whether confidence ratings differed among ontask, mind-blanking, daydream, and current state thought reports (as in Studies 1a and 1b). Mindblanking confidence was not significantly different than on-task confidence, t(107) = -2.59, p = .174, d = 0.25, BF10 = 2.552, daydream confidence, t(71) = 1.79, p = .931, d = 0.21, BF10 = 0.539, or current state confidence, t(77) = 0.69, p = .100, d = 0.08, BF10 = 0.156, with generally modest evidence that the data were more likely under than null than the alternative hypothesis for comparisons involving content-laden off-task reports. On-task confidence was statistically higher than that for current state, t(147) = 4.99, p < .001, d = 0.41, BF10 > 1000, and for daydream reports, t(112) = 4.89, p < .001, d = 0.46, BF10 > 1000. Unlike in Studies 1a and 1b, then, subjects were not significantly less confident in their mind-blanking reports than in their on-task reports, but of most importance, mind-blanking confidence was also at least as high as that for the other TUT categories, as it was in Studies 1a and 1b. Note: n = number of participants who made at least one report of the indicated thought response category.

We also preregistered an approach of comparing performance between subjects who reported any mind-blanking experiences versus those who reported no such experiences, rather than reporting a correlation between performance and mind-blanking rate as in Studies 1a and 1b. Post-SART Mind-Blanking Questionnaire

The post-SART exploratory question about mind-blanking experiences indicated that 62.1% of subjects (n = 329) endorsed that mind-blanking made sense to them and that they believe they have experienced it in daily life (compared to 68.5% from Study 1a). Only 6.4% of subjects reported that mind-blanking doesn't make sense to them and that they're skeptical that others experience it (compared to 7.1% in Study 1a).

Post-SART Sleepiness Ratings
