Since we had similar experimental designs across Studies 1a, 1b, and 2, we sought to maximize our statistical power by combining all three experiments to test for significant differences in mind-blanking counts between the conditions that did versus did not include an "I-

Discussion

Study 2 attempted to decrease rates of on-task thoughts by administering an easier, "vigilance" version of the SART and increasing its trial durations. Rates of on-task reports (Ms = .67-.69) declined modestly from those in Study 1a and 1b (where most condition Ms > .71). As in those prior studies, however, rates of mind-blanking (Ms = .05-.06) remained relatively low here, suggesting that this mental state is not frequently experienced (or, at least, reported) compared to all other content-laden off-task thoughts considered as a group.

We again found that the MB & IDK and MB but no IDK probe-type conditions did not differ significantly in predicting the log counts of mind-blanking reports (either in Study 2 or in our combined-study analysis). In contrast, the IDK but no MB condition was associated with a significantly higher log count of I-don't-know responses than was the MB & IDK condition in Study 2. This hypothesis-supporting finding should be taken lightly, however, because our crossexperiment, large-N analysis aligned with the findings of Study 1a and 1b did not produce a significant effect of probe-type condition on I-don't-know response counts. Again, if there is an actual effect of probe type in the population, it must be weak and unreliable, with our samples in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 (separately and combined) failing to produce it. These repeated null results imply that mind-blanking reports are unlikely to generally reflect meta-awareness failures, or Idon't-know experiences.

Confidence ratings for mind-blanking reports were again high in Study 2, indicating that subjects generally felt certain about their reports, contrary to our hypotheses. We also found, again, that mind-blanking reports were made with similar confidence to other off-task thought categories (i.e., current state of being and daydreams), and again there was no significant correlation between the frequency of mind-blanking reports and their confidence ratings.

Analyses of RTs to thought probes showed that mind-blanking-report latencies were not significantly longer (and were mostly numerically shorter) than other TUT category reports. As in Study 1a and Study 1b, this conflicts with our hypothesis that mind-blanking reports might reflect subjects trying and failing to retrieve a clear experience and then defaulting to a claim of "blanking," which should take more time than successfully and directly retrieving an experience such as daydreaming or worrying about the future. Instead, it appears that subjects apprehended an experience of "nothingness" similarly to recognizing a content-laden experience.

As in Study 1a, most subjects selected among the post-SART response choices that the mind-blanking phenomenon "makes sense" to them and that they have experienced it in everyday life. Very few subjects were skeptical of the phenomenon. And, consistent with Studies Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 55 1a and 1b, the Kendall's tau correlation was significant between mind-blanking rate and selfreported sleepiness.

The only replicated finding in Study 2 that may be problematic for the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports is that performance indicators in the "vigilance" SART (dʹ and response bias) did not correlate significantly with mind-blanking rate. As we speculated previously, however, the low prevalence of mind-blanking, even for those who experienced it more frequently than did others, probably limited the measurable impact of mind-blanking task performance.

An additional possibility, proposed by Boulakis and Demertzi (2025), is that mindblanking might often represent only brief transitional periods between content-laden conscious states; if so, this might limit their negative impact on performance (but see Ward & Wegner, 2013). This lack of impact on performance might be especially likely on a relatively easy task, with few target events, such as the one used here. Indeed, with the vigilance SART in Study 2, we did not find significant correlations between TUT rate and performance, either.

Overall, then, Study 2 replicated our findings from Study 1a and Study 1b suggesting that most subjects do not seem to be mis-categorizing I-don't-know experiences as mind-blanking reports: (a) We found no significant differences in the predicted log counts of mind-blanking between conditions that included versus excluded the "I-don't-know" response option (even in a cross-experiment analysis with a very large sample size), and; (b) Subjects' high confidence ratings and TUT-like RTs for mind-blanking reports suggested that they were not merely expressing uncertainty about their thoughts. The latter findings may be particularly important because they are less vulnerable to the criticism that low rates of mind-blanking and I-don'tknow reports across all our experiments may have made it difficult to statistically detect probetype condition differences in these counts.

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 56

Study 3

The current studies provide evidence that mind-blanking reports are not simply "I-don'tknow" experiences that subjects have miscategorized. Lingering skepticism about construct validity may still be warranted, however, until it is clearer what subjects mean phenomenologically when they report mind-blanking. As others have argued (Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Fell, 2022), "mind-blanking" in the psychological and neuroscience literatures has been defined and probed in multiple ways, such that mind-blanking reports may reflect an actual absence of experience, or instead, an incomplete awareness of experience, or no semantically identifiable "thought," or simply low alertness (or, perhaps, a linguistically inaccessible or unreportable state; see Kaufmann et al., 2024). A recently designed self-report scale, the Mind Blanking Questionnaire (Kawagoe et al., 2024), includes items that reflect either an absence of thought or experience altogether ("There are moments when my mind goes completely blank"; "There are moments when my mind empties out"), or instead, not remembering one's thoughts or not attending to one's actions ("There are moments that I can't remember what I was thinking about"; "I find myself not knowing what I was doing even though I wasn't thinking about anything else").

Forgetting one's thoughts or experiences is different from not having them at all.

Further heterogeneity is evident in the rising use of "blank mind" and "mind blanking" in everyday discourse, which may reflect what subjects mean when they report blanking in experiments (non-personalized Google searches of "blank mind" and "mind blanking" yielded 529,000 and 53,100 results, respectively; September 16, 2026). For example, the "blank" in mind-blanking might refer to a foggy experience without a clear focus, but with a sense of experiencing the world consciously, rather than as an absolute absence of any subjective experience. A theme that emerges from online subreddits about mental health has linked mindblanking (or "mind blanking syndrome") to "brain fog," or feeling mentally sluggish with thoughts that are unclear or not easily accessible (e.g., https://www.reddit.com/r/Depersonalization/; https://www.reddit.com/r/Dissociation/).

Formal qualitative research studies, typically in the context of dissociation and depersonalization following trauma, yield similar characterizations of mind-blanking (or "compartmentalisation phenomenology;" Melegkovits et al., 2025), as sometimes a foggy state or as a kind of metacognitive failure to access prior experiences (or both). In Cernis et al. (2020), for example, all 12 subjects reported some feelings of phenomenological detachment, described in various ways, including blanking (e.g., in a "box" [participant P8], in a "bubble" [P4], behind "a layer of Perspex" [P8], "murky" [P6], "numb...blank...dead to feelings" [P2] ).

An intensive qualitative exploration of mind-blanking experiences has recently emerged from descriptive experience sampling (DES) research. DES involves subjects wearing an earpiece that beeps unpredictably as a signal to take immediate stock of, and write notes on, their inner experience at the instant before the beep (e.g., Hurlburt, 1990 Hurlburt, , 2011;; Hurlburt & Heavey, 2006b). Participants complete comprehensive interviews at the end of the sampling day to discuss each beeped experience, and follow-up questions clarify the experience with as little bias as possible. A DES collaboration with the participant Mel May provides a rare example of someone frequently reporting no conscious experience across beeps (Hurlburt & Bass-Krueger, 2024). These reports are important, first, because they were not suggested by the study instructions, measurement items, or interview questions, or by the participant being part of a community centered around dissociation or depersonalization, and so they are unlikely to have

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 58 been influenced by demand characteristics.foot_1 Second, Mel's reports demonstrate a varied account of what experiencing a blank mind, or "nothing," is like; for Mel, mind-blanking is not only one kind of experience. Most striking, perhaps, is that Mel reports at nine beeps (not including the first "practice" sampling day) that she was having little to no inner experience at all and was, essentially, subjectively absent, despite engaging in some ongoing activity (beeps 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, 3.4, 4.2, 12.2, 13.3, 13.4): …this beep felt really nothing. And coming back to what I was saying earlier about like the word dormant feeling really nice, that's sort of what this experience felt like. There's nothing to latch onto in terms of trying to describe that…I'm not sure. I mean, I, I've, I would never say like a zero, but yeah, it didn't feel like there was anything happening that I could just like distinguish. (beep 2.3)

At other times, however, Mel expresses experiencing degrees of nothingness when engaged in well-practiced actions, such as vacuuming, consuming social media, or emailing (beeps 2.2, 3.3, 3.5, 5.3, 5.4, 6.3, 6.4, 6.6, 7.2, 10.1). Mel sometimes indicates, in these instances, an awareness of "just doing" the action, as if on "autopilot," but without any other thoughts, feelings, or experiences; she is subjectively present to some degree (e.g., "I'm still kind of present within the room" [beep 3.4]), but in a decidedly limited way.

I actually wasn't really taking in the content that I was looking at, to be honest… I think taking it in to some degree, but like way less…Yeah. Very lightly… It's not fully nothing…definitely my eyeballs are pointed at and the taking in something, but like, at a far less level than the other. (beep 6.4)

And at other times, still, Mel reports a sense of blanking or autopilot while she also has some degree of sensory awareness, experiencing visual, auditory, or tactile qualities to varying degrees, such as a chill on her legs (beeps 3.5, 5.4, 6.1, 6.4, 12.5, 12.6). Hurlburt et al. (2009) noted that DES subjects frequently hesitate to report sensory experiences, and often do so sheepishly or ambivalently, as if these experiences don't "count" because they focus on surfaces and lack semantic content. Perhaps these often register as "blanks" to some research participants.

All the evidence above suggests that interpretations of a "blank mind"-by laypeople, trauma patients, research subjects, and cognitive scientists-are potentially confounded by diverse assumptions, understandings, and metacognitive styles, leading to conceptual ambiguity, incomplete or faulty self-reports, and potentially inappropriate scientific conclusions (see also Fell, 2022). Study 3 sought to clarify what subjects mean when they report mind-blanking to thought probes during ongoing tasks. Specifically, we separated the mind-blanking response option from Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 into two separate, more phenomenologically specific options: "unclear/foggy" and "absent/no experience at all."

Study 3 thus aimed to advance our understanding of whether mind-blanking reports more typically attempt to convey the complete absence of experience or thought, or rather, to reflect a cloudier, less focused experience with no specific or clear thought content, but still with some subjectivity (Fell, 2022).

Study 3 administered the vigilance SART from Study 2, interrupted by probes that replaced the mind-blanking option with "unclear/foggy" and "absent/no experience at all." There were no probe manipulations in Study 3, as we were simply interested in whether subjects typically report one of these varieties of "mind-blanking" more often than the other, and whether subjects' confidence ratings in these reports would be similar across both report types.

Method

Study 3 received ethics approval from the UNC Greensboro IRB (via modification of protocol number 23-378). It was conducted after Study 2, but it was not preregistered (the last author accidentally failed to post a drafted preregistration document to OSF before participant testing began).

Sample Size Justification

We aimed to collect data from 400 subjects. For a paired t-test comparing dependent means (i.e., comparing unclear/foggy report rates to absent/no experience report rates), a sample of 400 subjects yields 80% power for d = .14, 90% power for d = .16, and 95% power for d = .18 (alpha = .05, two-tailed).

Subjects Before exclusions, 446 Prolific subjects completed Study 3. Subjects who took part in Study 1a, Study 1b, or Study 2 were not eligible; other prescreening criteria followed those from the prior studies. Subjects' average age (after exclusions) was M = 30.31 years, SD = 5.84. The post-exclusions sample was 52% female, 47% male, and 1% gender nonconforming; it was 61% White, 29% African American, 5% multiracial, 2% Hispanic or Latino, 1% East Asian, and less than 1% South Asian, Middle Eastern, or Native or Alaskan American. One subject identified (via free response) as simply "Asian" and another input their subject ID rather than using the provided response options. Subjects were paid $7.75 upon completion. Vigilance SART Subjects completed the same Vigilance SART as in Study 2, but with modified thought probes and instructions. The program for Study 3 is openly available at: https://app.gorilla.sc/openmaterials/859045. Thought Probes All subjects received the same probe response options: 1. The task/task performance, 2. Everyday things/personal worries, 3. Current state of being, 4. Daydreams/fantasies, 5. External environment, 6. Unclear/foggy, 7. Absent/no experience at all, 8. Other. In this study, then, the mind-blanking phenomenon was separated into two response options: "unclear/foggy" and Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 61 "absent/no experience at all." Hereafter, for simplicity, we will sometimes refer to Option 7 (absent/no experience at all) as "absent." All thought probes were followed by the confidence rating menu used in the MB but no IDK conditions from Studies 1a, 1b, and 2. Procedures The procedures for Study 3 matched Study 2, with the following exceptions. Two thought-type definitions were added to instructions corresponding to the new probe response options. Subjects received the following verbatim instructions for the unclear/foggy option: "Select this if you experienced a diffuse or foggy state that wasn't really 'about' anything clear or particular, but you were still having some sort of conscious experience or awareness." The description for the absent/no experience at all response option was, "Select this if you were experiencing nothing at all; your consciousness was completely absent, with no sensations, awareness, or any other experiences."

To facilitate subjects reading the probe response-option definitions carefully, the minimum durations of the on-screen instructions' descriptions of each thought type were increased. In this study, subjects were able to advance to the next instruction screen only after 3000 ms had elapsed (rather than 1500 ms previously).

Results

Exclusion criteria were the same as those from Studies 1a, 1b, and 2. Data from 7 subjects were dropped because they responded "extremely" to at least two of the three post-SART questions regarding their subjective state or immediate environment, or because they responded with "most of the time" or "all of the time" to at least one of the three mediamultitasking questions, or both. We dropped data from 24 other subjects because they responded to fewer than 30 thought probes. After exclusions, the total sample size was N = 415.

Thought-Report Rates

Retained subjects responded to M = 35.18 (SD = 1.26) probes of the 36 presented. Table 9 presents the mean rates of all endorsed mental states for Study 3. For unclear/foggy experiences, the M rate = .026, with 30.1% of subjects reporting this to at least one probe. Absent experiences were rarer, M rate = .011, and with only 15.9% reporting this to at least one probe. A total of 13.5% of subjects reported both unclear/foggy and absent experiences at least once, whereas 32.8% reported either an unclear/foggy or absent experience at least once. (Because most subjects reported no instances of either unclear/foggy or absent experiences, we did not analyze the correlation between their rates; any significant correlation would be driven by the overabundance of zeros on both variables.)

A paired samples t-test indicated a significantly higher reporting rate for unclear/foggy than absent states, t(414) = 5.99, p < .001, d = 0.29, 95% CI [0.20, 0.39], BF10 > 1000. Since both response rates were again highly skewed (see Figure 6 for distributions, along with on-task and daydream report rates for comparison), we also conducted paired Mann-Whitney U tests, which similarly indicated a significant difference between report rates, U = 6328.00, p < .001.

Note that, together, M reporting rates for unclear/foggy and absent experiences summed to a value that was close to-but a bit lower than-the rates of mind-blanking reports in the MB but no IDK conditions from Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 (.037 here, versus .043, .053, and .064, respectively). ("Unclear"), and absent/no experience at all ("Absent") report rates in Study 3. Experience At All ("Absent") Reports in Study 3.

For subjects who made at least one unclear/foggy report, the correlation with confidence rating was significantly positive, τ(123) = .30, p < .001, indicating that subjects who reported unclear/foggy experiences more frequently did so with greater confidence. The corresponding correlation between absent/no experience report rate and confidence ratings was not significant, however, τ(64) = .08, p = .403 (albeit with only half the sample size); this null finding more closely parallels the null correlations for mind-blanking report rates and confidence in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2.

Probe Report RT

Mean thought-report latencies for each probe response category are presented in Table 11. We conducted paired t-tests (with Holm corrections) to contrast thought types of interest.

Absent and unclear/foggy report RTs did not differ significantly from one another, t(55) = 1.45, p = 1.00, d = 0.19, BF10 = 0.392, with a BF approaching moderate evidence for the null relative to the alternative hypothesis. Absent report RTs were only significantly longer than on-task reports, t(59) = 7.00, p < .001, d = 0.90, BF10 > 1000. Unclear/foggy report RTs were also Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 67 significantly longer than on-task reports, t(116) = 9.11, p < .001, d = 0.84, BF10 > 1000, and everyday-things reports, t(100) = 3.38, p = .023, d = 0.34, BF10 = 21.283. Unclear/foggy and absent report RTs were not significantly different from any of the other content-laden off-task categories (all ts < 2.45, all ps > .126, all ds < 0.60, all BFs < .129), with at least modest evidence favoring the null over the alternative hypothesis.

SART Performance

We took the same approach here as in Study 2: Subjects' data from performance-based analyses were dropped if their target accuracy rate (go trials) was 3*IQR below the grand mean, and data for any subjects whose value was outside the Median +/-3*IQR were censored to the Median +/-3*IQR.

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 68

The mean dʹ score was 2.63 (SD = 1.09); dʹ did not correlate significantly with rates of unclear/foggy reports, τ(413) = -.04, p = .233, or absent reports, τ(413) = .00, p = .881.

Similarly, β scores (M = 7.47, SD = 12.01) were not significantly correlated with either unclear/foggy report rates, τ(413) = -.05, p = .213, or absent rates, τ(413) = .00, p = .916.

Consistent with the vigilance SART data from Study 2, TUT rates (M = .25, SD = .28) also didn't correlate significantly with performance measures, for dʹ, r(413) = -.03, p = .583, or β, r(413) = -.05, p = .269.

Post-SART Sleepiness Ratings

The weak significant correlation between sleepiness ratings and mind-blanking rates that we found in Study 1a, Study 1b, and Study 2 (see also Madiouni et al., 2020), replicated for unclear/foggy report rates, τ(413) = .13, p = .004, but not absent rates, τ(413) = .04, p = .408.

Discussion

Study 3 extended our investigation into the validity of mind-blanking reports by separating the mind-blanking response option into "unclear or foggy thoughts" versus "complete absence of experience" to decipher what subjects mean when they report mind-blanking (Fell, 2022). Unclear thoughts accounted for an average of 3% of reports, versus 1% of reports reflecting a complete absence of thought or subjective experience, reflecting a statistically significant difference in reporting rates (which was also representative of more subjects reporting any unclear/foggy experience than any absent experience). The distribution of mean response rates across the two new "mind-blanking" options mirrored the overall mind-blanking rates observed in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 reasonably closely, which averaged between 4%-6%.

Together, then, these findings provisionally suggest that mind-blanking reports (and perhaps experiences) more often reflect diffuse than absent subjective states, and so they aren't as phenomenologically "blank" as sometimes assumed. Indeed, perhaps the strongest takeaway here should be that, when given an option to distinguish a truly blank mind from a foggier conscious state, very few participants reported a complete absence of experience. If a truly "blank" mind sometimes happens, it may happen only rarely to only few participants.

Confidence ratings for both unclear and absent reports were generally high in Study 3, suggesting that subjects were reasonably certain about both possible forms of mind-blanking.

Although ratings were slightly lower for unclear/foggy than absent reports, this difference (and those with other off-task thought categories) was not statistically significant, and BFs reflected modest evidence favoring the null over the alternative hypothesis. As well, subjects reported these more specified forms of mind-blanking experiences with similar confidence as they generally reported for "mind-blanking" in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2. Finally, with respect to confidence ratings, there was a moderate positive correlation between the frequency of unclear reports and their confidence ratings in Study 3, but the correlation was not present for absent reports, which may be attributable to the limited number of subjects who made such reports (n = 66). The positive correlation involving unclear/foggy reports and confidence was not seen for mind-blanking reports in Studies 1a, 1b, or 2, and so it will be important to replicate this analysis in future studies; for now, it suggests that either confidence may grow in unclear/foggy reports as these experiences accumulate, or people who are more confident about their unclear/foggy experiences are more likely to select that response option.

Just as in the Study 2 analysis of mind blanking, performance indicators from the vigilance SART (dʹ and response bias) did not correlate significantly with either variety of mind blanking (unclear/foggy or absent reports); they also didn't correlate with TUT rates reflecting content-laden experiences. Unclear/foggy report rates were weakly positively correlated with sleepiness ratings; absent report rates were not, and so this finding should also be a target for replication in future work, especially because "mind blanking" reports in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 were significantly correlated with sleepiness. The sleepiness correlations here further suggest that when subjects report mind blanking to probes, they often mean to convey a foggy or otherwise nondescript phenomenology rather than the absence of any experience. Finally, analyses of response latencies to thought-probe screens showed that unclear/foggy and absent experiences did not differ significantly in their reporting RTs. They were both longer than ontask thought reports, but not different from current state or daydream RTs. As in our prior experiments, then, mind-blanking reports were not made especially slowly, as one would expect if those reports were reflective of subjects defaulting to a mind-blanking response only after trying and failing to recall their previous experience.

We think it worth reiterating that the combined rates of unclear/foggy reports and completely-absent reports in Study 3 sum to about the rates of "blank mind" reports in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2s, suggesting that they may have captured much of the phenomenological ground normally attributed to mind-blanking. Moreover, these two report types also traded-off correlational patterns that were like versus unlike those involving mind-blanking reports: Like mind-blanking rates, absent report rates did not correlate significantly with confidence, whereas unclear/foggy reports did; like mind-blanking rates, absent report rates correlated significantly with sleepiness ratings, whereas unclear/foggy reports did not. It seems possible that "blank mind" reports made in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 reflected a mix (within and/or across subjects) of unclear/foggy and completely-absent experiences, with one or the other driving the correlational patterns with other variables.

General Discussion

We conducted four online studies to better understand the subjective experiences that lead subjects to report mind-blanking to thought probes during cognitive tasks. Do mindblanking reports reflect confident commitments to having had no conscious thoughts or experiences, or might they (at least sometimes, or for some people) be used to convey a lack of awareness or an uncertainty about prior subjective states (Mathews et al., 2024), or to communicate vague or foggy experiences with little identifiable semantic or perceptual content?

Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 tested whether failures of meta-consciousness, or I-don't-know experiences, are sometimes reported as mind-blanking, using three experimental conditions that differed in response options to thought probes that were presented unpredictably during an attention task. We expected mind-blanking rates to selectively drop when thought probes offered subjects an "I-don't-know" response option. If so, this would have suggested that subjects sometimes inaccurately reported experiences of mind-blanking due to the forgetting of, or uncertainty about, their previous thoughts.

We were wrong: There were no significant differences in the predicted log counts of mind-blanking reports between conditions that included versus excluded the "I-don't-know" response option. In other words, having an "I-don't-know" response option available did not reduce mind-blanking reports, and so subjects did not appear to be misinterpreting I-don't-know experiences as mind-blanking. Subjects were, moreover, highly confident in their mind-blanking reports in all three studies, and as confident as they were about content-laden TUT experiences.

They also made their mind-blanking reports as quickly as they made their other TUT reports.

Both the confidence and latency findings are consistent with blanking experiences being as immediately apprehended as content-laden off-task thoughts and they are inconsistent with blanking reports being made only after one has tried and failed to retrieve an experience. (And, as noted below, both specified varieties of "mind-blanking" that were probed in Study 3 showed similar patterns of confidence and response latency.)

Our initial hypothesis, that mind-blanking reports often reflect subjects' uncertainty about their prior conscious states, would have been further supported if I-don't-know report rates significantly increased in the condition that did not also include a "blank mind" response option.

In fact, I-don't-know response counts were also unexpectedly similar between probe-type conditions, suggesting that mind-blanking reports were not coming from meta-consciousness failures. I-don't-know report counts were extremely low in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2, however, making statistical comparisons between probe-type conditions difficult.

The evidence summarized above, from Studies 1a, 1b, and 2, supports the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports, insofar as they don't appear to reflect I-don't-know experiences in disguise. Moreover, the results seem to fit with other relevant behavioral and neurophysiological findings in the literature that we reviewed in the Introduction, including our (weak) positive correlation between mind-blanking rates and sleepiness ratings. There appears to be something distinct about the experiences that precipitate mind-blanking reports versus content-laden mind-wandering reports, and it's not simply uncertainty.

In our view, however, significant questions-if not concerns-remain. For example, dropping the "blank mind" response option in Studies 1a, 1b, or 2 did not systematically increase rates of I-don't-know or Other responses. It is not clear, then, how mind-blanking experiences were reported when "blank mind" was not provided as a response option, as rates of the other thought-content reports also did not systematically change across probe-type conditions in these experiments. The most plausible explanation might come from considering the results of our final study (Study 3), discussed below, which also may generally suggest a new, alternate interpretation of what "mind-blanking" means to at least some participants.

Inconsistent (or Inappropriate) Operational Definitions and Fruitful Future Directions

Some researchers define mind-blanking as the inability to report immediately preceding mental content (Boulakis et al. 2023), suggesting that mind-blanking reports may reflect I-don'tknow (or I-don't-remember) experiences. Others, however, define mind-blanking as a lack of conscious awareness, during which the individual is not focally aware of any stimuli, either internal or external (Ward and Wegner, 2013). Some operationalizations even combine these two (Kawagoe et al. 2024) or combine them with other types of experience, such as feeling unalert (Robison & Unsworth, 2018). Consequently, not all studies provide identical definitions of mind-blanking to research subjects to instruct them when (or why) to report it (see Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Fell, 2022). Some studies ask subjects to report mind-blanking when they have no thoughts (Kawagoe et al., 2019; Ward & Wegner, 2013), whereas others require mindblanking to be reported either if subjects fail to remember mental content or if they have no thoughts (Koroma et al., 2023; Palhares et al., 2026). Finally, although some studies have distinguished between unsure and mind-blanking experiences in their reporting instructions and thought probes, the analyses subsequently combined these report types (Andrillion et al. 2019; Corcoran et al., 2025; Palhares et al., 2026).

Diverse definitions of mind-blanking-in the scientific literature and in instructions to research subjects-threaten the construct validity of mind-blanking reports (Boulakis & Demertzi, 2025; Fell, 2022). In mind-wandering investigations, researchers rely on operationalization to efficiently communicate with each other and with research subjects (Seli et al. 2018a (Seli et al. , 2018b)). The same is required for mind-blanking research.

Our Study 3 thus explored the phenomenology that drives people's probed mind-blanking reports. Based on suggestive results from descriptive and qualitative studies (e.g., Cernis et al., 2020; Hurlburt & Bass-Krueger, 2024), we replaced the previous "blank mind" response option with two others, "unclear/foggy" and "absent/no experience at all." The former allowed subjects to indicate that they were having some kind of subjective experience, even if it was diffuse or not clear in semantic or perceptual content (perhaps similar to what is colloquially described as "brain fog"), whereas the latter specified and emphasized a complete absence of thought and subjective experience, which is implied by most scientific discussions of mind-blanking since Ward and Wegner (2013). Whereas in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2, our task instructions defined blanking for participants as, "You were not thinking about the task or anything else at all-Your mind was a complete blank," in line with prior research, the Study 3 instructions emphasized further the absence of all conscious experience, "…you were experiencing nothing at all; your consciousness was completely absent, with no sensations, awareness, or any other experiences."

We found that subjects reported both forms of mind-blanking, with unclear/foggy experiences having significantly higher report rates (3%) than did absent experiences (1%). This finding preliminarily suggests that mind-blanking may have (at least) two sub-varieties or subjective interpretations; indeed, 13.5% of the sample in Study 3 reported at least one instance of both "blanking" experiences, suggesting that they were willing and able to discriminate between the two. If researchers are interested in better understanding the concept and phenomenology of mind-blanking, then, they may want to distinguish between its ostensible unclear/foggy and absent/no-experience forms or, perhaps, test whether additional (or alternative) dimensions might also be reliably reportable. At the very least, further work is now needed to assess the reliability and construct validity of probed unclear/foggy and completelyabsent reports, as well as reports of any related varieties of mind-blanking.

For now, though, our Study 3 findings indicate that only a small proportion of participants sometimes report a complete absence of experience, and when they do, they rate their confidence as high as for content-laden mind-wandering experiences. The fact that truly absent experiences were only reported 1% of the time, on average, suggests that when most subjects reported mind-blanking in our prior studies (and perhaps in other studies, as well), they didn't mean they lacked conscious awareness of anything at all; instead, they may have meant that they could not identify their thoughts or experiences have having semantic or perceptual content. Unclear or foggy experiences may be behind most probed reports of mind-blanking. If this is correct, it suggests an explanation for our finding that mind-blanking reports did not clearly migrate to any other particular response category when probes did not include a "blank mind" option: Subjects may have been able to translate their unclear or foggy experiencewhich did not reflect a complete absence of awareness-to the available content-laden TUT category that provided the closest approximation to their ambiguous conscious state.

Constraints on Generality

Our provisional conclusions about the nature of mind-blanking and the construct validity of probed mind-blanking reports, and our recommendations for future research, are based on four experimental studies conducted in an online attention-task context with Prolific participants living in the United States. Mean rates of mind-blanking reports might have been higher in laboratory contexts, where there is less potential for environmental distractions, and with laboratory participants, who may be less concerned than Prolific participants that off-task thought reports might affect their compensation; other types of ongoing tasks, perhaps more Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 76 familiar ones affording automaticity of responding, might also yield higher reporting rates of mind-blanking and other off-task experiences. If so, then laboratory settings and simpler tasks might allow more powerful tests of probe-type differences in mind-blanking reporting rates (assuming large enough participants samples are tested in the laboratory).

Our present construct validity tests were limited to three experiments contrasting mindblanking rates between conditions that did versus did not offer an "I-don't-know" response option, and one experiment distinguishing unclear/foggy experiences from the complete absence of any experience. Yet, as noted above, other varieties or interpretations of mind-blanking might also be examined. One potential alternative conception of blanking is the phenomenon of "just doing," which, as far as we're aware, has only been discussed deeply in the context of DES findings. DES investigations have characterized "just doing" as having one's awareness being occupied only by the activity in which one is engaged (e.g., "just" buttering toast without any other thoughts or awareness, or "just" watching TV; Hurlburt & Heavey, 2006a). Hurlburt et al. (2002), for example, found that students with high speech rates reported "just doing" much more frequently (13.3% of DES samples) than did those with moderate or low speech rates (2.9% of samples); some of Mel May's "autopilot" experiences also seem consistent with the phenomenology of "just doing" (Hurlburt & Bass-Krueger, 2024) On one hand, because "just doing" experiences don't seem to come along with any other phenomenology beyond the ongoing behaviors, it's possible that research participants who are "just doing" the SART, or "just reading" War & Peace, might sometimes report these experiences as mind-blanking. On the other hand, because "just doing" experiences are typically described as involving awareness of the ongoing activity, it seems equally plausible that participants who are "just doing" their task might often report these as "on-task" experiences. It

Validity of Probed Mind-Blanking Reports 77 will take additional construct-validation work to determine whether laboratory subjects sometimes experience "just doing," and whether or how they might faithfully report it to thought probes. 5 Finally, by relying on thought-probe methods with fixed response options, our study was limited in what it could explore and conclude about the nature and phenomenology of mindblanking experiences. Subjects could only report using the options we offered them, and some reports could have been affected by demand characteristics to use some or all the provided response options at some point in the experiment. More open-ended qualitative or descriptive research approaches, particularly those collecting in-the-moment reports rather than retrospective reports, might be particularly valuable in such future explorations of the "blank" mind and its varieties. Although some of the "blank" and "absent" reports offered by the DES participant Mel May that we reviewed (Hurlburt & Bass-Krueger, 2024) might be interpreted as "just doing" or "sensory awareness" experiences, the field should not ignore that some of her other reports clearly and confidently convey a complete absence of phenomenology, suggesting that "absent" experiences are possible and worthy of further investigation.

Such future qualitative and quantitative research, moreover, should be conducted across cultures and populations that might have different folk beliefs about consciousness, or different reporting biases, or both. Although mind-blanking research has been conducted in Japan 5 The "just doing" phenomenology seems to share a family resemblance with "flow" experiences (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990), in that they involve little awareness of stimuli or thoughts beyond the ongoing activity. Flow, however, is an "optimal" and often exhilarating experience, conceived as accompanying activities that are especially valued and engaging (and that match challenge with ability). Thus, flow is unlikely to be experienced by people buttering toast, watching TV, reading War & Peace on-screen for research credit, or pressing the spacebar in an online SART; e.g., Warm et al., 2008 Warm et al., , 2015)), and so flow may be fundamentally different than "just doing." In creative activities that might inspire flow, however, some participants might select a "mindblanking" thought-probe response option as closer to their subjective experience than is an "on task" option (e.g., Palhares et al., 2026). (Kawagoe et al., 2018; 2019; 2024), as well as in Europe (e.g., Boulakis et al., 2023; Koroma et al., 2023; Mortaheb et al., 2022) and North America (e.g., Beikmohamadi & Meier, 2024; Ward & Wegner, 2013), this represents a limited participant pool to establish the validity of a fascinating and potentially underappreciated state of consciousness.

Conclusions

Within the constraints and limitations acknowledged above, our findings from Studies 1a, 1b, and 2 provide significant evidence against our hypothesis that participants' mind-blanking reports represented a failure to remember previous subjective experience. Mind-blanking reports: (a) did not decrease when participants were provided with a thought-probe option to indicate that they could not remember their preceding thoughts; (b) elicited confidence ratings that were numerically and categorically high (averaging between 3.5-4 on a 5-point scale, between the scale labels, "confident" and "very confident"), similar to those elicited by content-laden TUT reports, and; (c) were made with similar latencies as content-laden TUT reports.

If we are wrong, however, and mind-blanking reports did primarily reflect I-don't-know experiences that participants mischaracterized, then all of the following would need to be true: (a) participants chose not to use the available "I-don't-know" response option to report these experiences, despite prior mind-wandering research indicating that participants are quite willing to report such memory failures (Mathews et al., 2024; Yeo et al., 2026); (b) participants chose to report high confidence in their mind-blanking reports despite their not actually remembering what they had experienced, and; (c) the response threshold for failing to recall one's experience and then making an attribution (i.e., to indicate a negative/"absence") is no higher-and its response latency is no longer-than that for recalling and reporting one's experience (i.e., to indicate a positive/"presence"), despite all three of our studies showing (non-significantly) longer report latencies-by 400 to 1400 ms-for I-don't-know reports than for mind-blanking reports.

Although any of these are possible, of course, we view their convergence here as implausible in the absence of supporting evidence.

Moreover, we interpret our findings across all our studies, including Study 3, to indicate that the field needs further construct validation research to properly characterize the experiences that lead people to report mind blanking. Based on findings from prior qualitative and descriptive research (e.g., Cernis et al., 2020; Hurlburt & Bass-Krueger, 2024), Study 3 thought probes allowed participants to report two varieties of "mind blanking," with only one of those representing an absence of subjective experience ("Absent/no experience at all" versus "Unclear/foggy"); participants rarely chose the no-experience option, suggesting that most mindblanking reports reflect some sort of conscious experience. Can we trust these findings? Can people accurately distinguish "foggy" from "absent" experiences? A considerable empirical literature indicates that participants can provide valid reports of different varieties of mindwandering content (e.g., Banks & Welhaf, 2021; Jordano & Touron, 2017; Kane, Gross et al., 2017; Kane, Smeekens et al., 2017; McVay et al., 2013; Mézière et al., 2025; Ruby et al., 2013; Smallwood et al., 2009 Smallwood et al., , 2011;; Welhaf & Banks, 2026; Welhaf et al., 2020). It's therefore possible they can also validly report varieties of mind blanking. Of course, this has yet to be independently demonstrated, and people may be better able to distinguish among content-laden TUT experiences more accurately than among experiences along some "absent"-"foggy"-"justdoing" continuum of mind-blanking. Whether unclear/foggy reports in Study 3 actually reflected unclear/foggy experiences, and whether typical "mind blanking" reports might frequently reflect unclear/foggy experiences (or completely absent experiences), will require further construct validation tests.

Authors' Contributions

Below we report our author contributions using CRediT.

Confidence Ratings

Subjects who endorsed at least one unclear/foggy experience (n = 125) were generally confident in their reports, with a rating M = 3.47. This is similar, but slightly lower than, confidence ratings for absent reports (n = 66), M = 3.77. Figure 7 shows raincloud plots for confidence ratings, where the modal rating M was 5.0 for absent reports (as it had been for mindblanking reports in Study 1a, 1b, and 2), but was 3.0 for unsure/foggy reports. See Table 10 for M confidence ratings for every thought-report category.

We used paired t-tests (with Holm corrections) to compare confidence ratings among ontask, unclear/foggy, absent, daydream, and current state thought reports (as in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2). Mean confidence ratings between unclear and absent reports were not significantly different, t(55) = 0.62, p = .100, d = 0.083, BF10 = 0.176, with modest evidence that the data were more likely under the null than the alternative hypothesis. In fact, confidence ratings for neither absent reports, nor unclear/foggy reports, differed significantly from any of those for the other off-task thought categories (all ts < 0.12, all ps > .05, all BF10 near or below 1). As in Studies 1a, 1b, and 2, then, subjects did not report blanking-type experiences with lower confidence than contentladen TUT experiences.
